title: Shillong horticulture & floriculture: a note to the credit manager
narrative:
## What the business physically is
**This is a perishable-crop business: seed or sapling plus polyhouse, water and labour go in, and cut flowers, vegetables and fruit come out within weeks, so cash arrives fast but spoils faster.** Value sits in the last mile — grading, cold storage and the buyer — not in the field. Capex is polyhouse, irrigation and a packhouse; the working-capital cycle is short on the sales side and long on the receivable side when selling to institutional buyers. **Price is set daily by the buyer, not the grower, and the government has ruled out a blanket support price for all farm produce [3], so there is no floor under a weak lot.** Collect from customer: current realisations per stem/kg, buyer mix and receivable days.

## What has changed now
**The state is promoting FTA-linked exports and pushing to reopen border haats with upgraded trade infrastructure along the Bangladesh border [1], which is a genuine new demand channel for graded produce.** A floriculture expo is running in Upper Shillong [2], which tells us the cluster is active but not that volumes or prices have risen. **The data pack gives no score for Meghalaya or the national benchmark [D], so we have no quantitative read on this city at all.** Sources say little specific to Shillong's own trade volumes; lean on first principles and on peers.

## What the peers say
**Peer results are mixed and mostly not Shillong: Pushpanjali Floriculture grew March 2026 net sales 40.95% year-on-year to Rs 13.18 crore but posted a quarterly net loss of Rs 2.15 crore and negative EBITDA of Rs 0.24 crore [6].** Nagarjuna Agri-Tech's June 2026 sales jumped to INR 321.81 million from INR 15.31 million a year ago [5], but its June 2026 EPS fell to -0.01 despite higher revenue of Rs 32 crore [7] — growth without profit. **Read this as: revenue growth in this sector is easy to buy and hard to convert to cash.** The rating-methodology sources [8][9][10][11] are generic and old; they give no sector number.

## Who to pursue, and how to grow safely
**Pursue growers with a written offtake or export order, at least two crops, and their own grading or cold room; avoid single-crop cut-flower growers selling into open mandis and traders with no land or packhouse.** When a proposal lands, check the offtake contract's buyer and penalty clause; if the buyer is a single unrated trader, ask for assignment of receivables or a tripartite confirmation. **Structure as a cash-flow loan sized to the crop cycle, not a term loan sized to the polyhouse.** Take every month: sales and realisation register, buyer-wise receivables ageing, power bills for the cold room, and a crop-condition note.

## Early-warning signs
**Watch for a shift from contracted buyers to mandi sales, receivables stretching past the crop cycle, and cold-room power bills falling while sales are claimed flat.** If receivables age past the cycle, stop enhancement and ask for the buyer's payment proof. If a borrower's crop mix narrows to one flower, cut limit and require crop insurance. If border-haat reopening slips, treat export-order projections as unconfirmed.
watch: Realisation below contract for two months -> freeze enhancement, review offtake
Bills fall while sales claimed flat -> inspect stock and stop disbursement
Single-crop concentration -> cut limit, require insurance
Border haat / FTA export order status (quarterly)
Reopening slips -> treat export projections as unconfirmed, resize
watch_note: Trigger levels are policy suggestions (analytical framing), not data.
